record.paper_title: Observational Cosmology: caveats and open questions in the standard model
record.original_question: Do absorption-line measurements in high-redshift clouds demonstrate that the cosmic microwave background radiation temperature increases with redshift as T proportional to 1 + z, or are those inferred temperatures too dependent on collisional excitation, ultraviolet pumping, infrared dust emission, and other local excitation mechanisms to serve as a definitive test?

evidence.quote: Therefore, previous works have not proven the increase of CMBR temperature with z by a factor (1 + z).
The result depends on the estimate of other contributions to the excitation, so nothing can yet be concluded definitively from this test.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
In the standard hot Big Bang cosmology, the cosmic microwave background (CMB) is predicted to be a blackbody whose temperature scales with redshift as
$$T_{\rm CMB}(z) = T_0\,(1+z),\qquad T_0 = 2.725\,\text{K}.$$
One observational test of this prediction uses quasar absorption-line systems at high redshift: the relative populations of fine-structure or rotational levels of species such as C I, C II, CN, CO, or H2O in intervening or associated clouds are measured, and an excitation temperature is inferred. If the CMB is the dominant excitation source, this excitation temperature equals $T_{\rm CMB}(z)$; otherwise additional local mechanisms (collisional excitation by particles in the cloud, ultraviolet pumping by ambient radiation, infrared pumping by dust emission, and other excitation channels) contribute and must be modeled and subtracted.

Question: Do the available absorption-line excitation-temperature measurements in high-redshift clouds constitute a definitive demonstration that $T_{\rm CMB}(z) = T_0(1+z)$, or are the inferred temperatures sufficiently dependent on the modeling of collisional excitation, UV pumping, IR dust emission, and other local excitation mechanisms that they cannot yet conclusively confirm or rule out this scaling law? More precisely, determine whether observations exist (or design observations) that establish the $(1+z)$ scaling of $T_{\rm CMB}$ from absorption-line data in a manner independent of, or robust to, uncertainties in such local excitation contributions.
artifact.status_search_result: Since 2003, absorption-line measurements have substantially improved. CO rotational excitation in quasar absorption systems up to z~3 (Noterdaeme et al. 2011) yields T_CMB(z) = 2.725(1+z)^{1-β} with β = -0.007 ± 0.027, consistent with the standard (1+z) scaling. A precise determination at z=0.89 (Muller et al. 2013) and an H2O absorption measurement at z=6.34 (Riechers et al. 2022) further support the linear scaling within errors. Local-excitation modeling (collisions, UV/IR pumping) remains a systematic that authors explicitly account for, but current constraints meaningfully confirm the (1+z) law in the redshift ranges probed; deviations are not detected and the original concern is partially resolved.

status_evidence.title: Measurements of TCMB at high redshift from CO excitation
status_evidence.claim: CO absorption measurements up to z~3 confirm the linear (1+z) scaling with high precision.

status_evidence.title: Microwave background temperature at z=6.34 from H2O absorption
status_evidence.snippet: Measurement of the CMB temperature using H2O absorption at z=6.34 is consistent with standard ΛCDM cosmology.
status_evidence.claim: Recent high-z absorption measurement consistent with (1+z) scaling.

status_evidence.title: A precise and accurate determination of the CMB temperature at z=0.89
status_evidence.snippet: Precise determination of TCMB at z=0.89 consistent with standard scaling.
status_evidence.claim: Improved precision measurement, consistent with T0(1+z).
